title: Modelling adaptation with the EvoDemo-Hyper MPM
text:
Welcome
This is a hands-on workshop for modelling how populations adapt to selection using the EvoDemo-Hyper matrix population model and its R package, evodemohypermpm.
The method bridges two traditions that have long talked past each other: demographers, who track populations through matrix models, and evolutionary quantitative geneticists, who track heritable traits through the breeder’s equation. The EvoDemo-Hyper MPM does both at once, in a single, fast, transparent matrix — and lets you ask questions like “which kind of species adapts fastest, and does the answer even have a single value?”
By the end you will be able to:

Anyone comfortable running R code who is curious about evolutionary demography. You do not need to know matrix algebra to get value from the 2-hour core — we run the model first and open the engine later. The “Going further” part is for those who want the machinery.

title: 1  The big picture
text:
1.1 Two ways of thinking about change
When a population meets a changing environment, two research communities reach for different tools.
Demographers describe a population as numbers of individuals in stages — juveniles, adults — and project them forward with a matrix population model (MPM). This captures the life cycle beautifully but, in its classic form, has no genetics: it cannot let a trait evolve.
Evolutionary quantitative geneticists describe a trait — its mean, its heritable (additive genetic) variance — and predict its response to selection with the breeder’s equation. This captures evolution but tends to flatten the life cycle into a single “generation”.
These two pictures have sometimes produced contradictory claims about how fast species adapt (Van de Walle et al. 2025). The EvoDemo-Hyper MPM dissolves the contradiction by doing both at once: it keeps the full life cycle of an MPM and lets a heritable trait evolve, in one matrix that is fast to compute and transparent to inspect.

title: 1  The big picture
text:
TipKey idea



The EvoDemo-Hyper MPM is an ordinary matrix model with two extra dimensions bolted on: besides stage, every individual also carries a breeding value (its heritable genetic contribution) and a phenotype. Selection reshapes the trait distribution; inheritance passes it to offspring.

title: 1  The big picture
text:
1.2 The life cycle
Everything in this workshop rests on one simple, two-stage life cycle: juveniles (J) and adults (A), censused just before breeding, with annual time steps.

flowchart LR
  J(("Juvenile<br/>J")) -->|"S_J · γ — mature"| A(("Adult<br/>A"))
  J -->|"S_J · (1−γ) — stay J"| J
  A -->|"S_A — survive"| A
  A -->|"F — reproduce"| J




flowchart LR
  J(("Juvenile<br/>J")) -->|"S_J · γ — mature"| A(("Adult<br/>A"))
  J -->|"S_J · (1−γ) — stay J"| J
  A -->|"S_A — survive"| A
  A -->|"F — reproduce"| J






Four vital rates govern the transitions:

\(S_J\) — juvenile survival,
\(S_A\) — adult survival,
\(\gamma\) — the probability a surviving juvenile matures into an adult,
\(F\) — fertility, the per-capita number of juveniles an adult contributes next year (\(F = f \times S_J\)).

Stacked into a projection matrix, the demography is just a \(2\times2\) Leslie matrix:
\[
\mathbf{A} =
\begin{pmatrix}
S_J(1-\gamma) & F \\[2pt]
S_J\,\gamma   & S_A
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
That is the entire demographic skeleton. The five species you will meet later differ only in the numbers that fill these four slots.

title: 1  The big picture
text:
1.3 Adding genetics
Now give every individual a quantitative trait \(z\) that influences one of the vital rates. Following the classic decomposition, the phenotype is a population mean plus a heritable breeding value and an environmental deviation:
\[
z = \bar{z} + a + e, \qquad V_P = V_A + V_E, \qquad h^2 = \frac{V_A}{V_P}.
\]
Here \(V_P\) is the phenotypic variance, \(V_A\) the additive genetic variance, and \(h^2\) the heritability — the fraction of trait variation that is passed on. Selection acts on \(z\); only the breeding value \(a\) is inherited.
The model discretises both the breeding value and the phenotype into a grid of classes (centred on zero, spanning \(\pm\) a range you choose). So instead of tracking “how many juveniles and adults”, it tracks how many individuals of each (stage, breeding value, phenotype) combination — a three-dimensional hyperstate. Offspring draw their breeding value from their parents via the Fisher infinitesimal model, which is how evolution enters.
You do not need the matrix algebra to use the model — we open that engine in Chapter 5. For now, hold on to this:






TipThe model in one sentence



Project a population through its life cycle, but on a grid of trait values, so that selection bends the trait distribution one way and inheritance passes the bent distribution to the next generation — and read off both population dynamics and trait evolution from the same run.








ImportantYour turn — make a prediction



A fast-living grass and a slow-living albatross face the same selection pressure on the same heritable trait. Which one do you expect to adapt faster per year? Write your guess down — we will test it in Chapter 4, and the answer is more interesting than it looks.






Van de Walle, Joanie, Jimmy Garnier, Timothée Bonnet, and Stephanie Jenouvrier. 2025. “Toward a Unified Approach to Modelling Adaptation Among Demographers and Evolutionary Ecologists.” Methods in Ecology and Evolution 16 (8): 1644–57. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.70075.

title: 2  Your first model
text:
2.1 One function, one projection
The whole model is driven by a single function, MPM(). We hand it the four vital rates, the genetics (\(h^2\), \(V_P\)), and the selection strength (\(\beta\)). Let’s project species 1 (a fast, grass-like life history) with selection acting on fertility — the package defaults.
out <- MPM(
  h2   = 0.2,            # heritability of the selected trait
  Vp   = 1,             # phenotypic variance
  Beta = 0.15,          # strength of selection (on the link scale)
  Fe   = species$F[1],      # fertility
  SA   = species$SA[1],     # adult survival
  SJ   = species$SJ[1],     # juvenile survival
  S0   = species$SJ[1],     # newborn survival (here equal to SJ)
  Y    = species$gamma[1],  # maturation rate
  selectedrate = "Fe"   # the vital rate selection acts on
)
That’s it — a deterministic eco-evolutionary projection over 100 years. (We pass S0 separately because the model lets newborn survival differ from later juvenile survival; here we keep them equal.)

The scalars T_GEN (generation time), LAMBDA0 (initial growth rate) and V (the mean change in breeding value per year — a realised adaptation rate).

title: 2  Your first model
text:
2.3 Plot 1 — the population grows

ggplot(out$properties_per_year, aes(year, N)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, colour = species_pal["1"]) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Population size", title = "Species 1 — population trajectory")







Figure 2.1: Population size over 100 years. With directional selection and no density dependence, the population grows without bound — that is expected, not a bug.











WarningHeads-up — exponential growth is by design



The model has no density dependence: selection raises \(\lambda\) above 1, so the population explodes. We care about the trait, not the absolute numbers. If you want a constant-size baseline, set enforce_initial_lambda1 = TRUE (it tunes fertility so the starting \(\lambda = 1\)).

title: 2  Your first model
text:
2.4 Plot 2 — the trait evolves
Here is the evolution half of the story: the mean breeding value climbs over time as selection favours individuals with higher trait values.






ImportantYour turn — predict first



Before running the next chunk: with positive selection on fertility, do you expect the mean breeding value to go up, down, or stay flat? Should adults and juveniles differ?



out$properties_per_year |>
  select(year, adult = M_EBVSA, juvenile = M_EBVSJ) |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "age_class", values_to = "mean_bv") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, mean_bv, colour = age_class)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = age_pal, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Mean breeding value", title = "Genetic change through time")







Figure 2.2: Mean breeding value of adults and juveniles. Selection drags the genetic mean upward; juveniles lead because they are the freshly-recruited, more-selected cohort.

title: 2  Your first model
text:
2.5 Plot 3 — the whole distribution sliding
Means hide the action. The trait distribution itself slides to the right as the population adapts. Plotting a few yearly snapshots makes the movement visible.

out$pheno_distribution |>
  filter(year %in% seq(1, 101, by = 20)) |>
  ggplot(aes(phenotypic_midvalue, density, colour = year, group = year)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1, name = "Year") +
  labs(x = "Phenotype value", y = "Density",
       title = "The trait distribution adapts over 100 years")







Figure 2.3: Phenotype distribution every 20 years. The hump shifts toward higher trait values — adaptation in motion.











TipKey idea



properties_per_year is your summary timeline; pheno_distribution is the full picture. Almost every figure in this workshop is one of these two objects, reshaped and plotted.

title: 2  Your first model
text:
2.6 Your turn — drive it yourself






ImportantExercise




Re-run the projection for the albatross (species 5) instead of the grass. Which species$ columns change?
Then set Beta = 0 and re-run. Predict what the breeding-value plot will look like before you draw it.









CautionSolution






alba <- MPM(
  h2 = 0.2, Vp = 1, Beta = 0.15,
  Fe = species$F[5], SA = species$SA[5], SJ = species$SJ[5],
  S0 = species$SJ[5], Y = species$gamma[5], selectedrate = "Fe"
)

no_sel <- MPM(
  h2 = 0.2, Vp = 1, Beta = 0,            # selection switched off
  Fe = species$F[5], SA = species$SA[5], SJ = species$SJ[5],
  S0 = species$SJ[5], Y = species$gamma[5], selectedrate = "Fe"
)

no_sel$properties_per_year |>
  ggplot(aes(year, M_EBVSA)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, colour = "grey40") +
  ylim(-4, 4) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Mean breeding value (adults)",
       title = "No selection \u2192 no genetic change")








With Beta = 0 the mean breeding value stays flat: no selection, no adaptation. This is the sanity check every eco-evolutionary model should pass.

title: 3  Selection scenarios
text:
3.1 A helper to run one scenario
Selection does not have to act on fertility. The selectedrate argument lets you choose which vital rate the trait influences: "Fe" (fertility), "SJ" (juvenile survival), "SA" (adult survival) or "Y" (maturation). Everything else stays the same — so any difference we see is about the life cycle position of the trait, not about the genetics.
We’ll work with species 3 (a passerine-like, intermediate life history) so all four scenarios are well behaved.
Rather than copy-paste the call four times, wrap it once and vary only selectedrate:
run_scenario <- function(rate, sp = 3) {
  MPM(
    h2 = 0.2, Vp = 1, Beta = 0.15,
    Fe = species$F[sp], SA = species$SA[sp], SJ = species$SJ[sp],
    S0 = species$SJ[sp], Y = species$gamma[sp],
    selectedrate = rate
  )
}

rates <- c("Fe", "SJ", "SA", "Y")
runs  <- set_names(rates) |> map(run_scenario)   # one MPM run per vital rate
runs is now a named list of four projections. We bind their yearly timelines into one tidy frame:
prop_all <- imap_dfr(runs, \(out, rate)
  out$properties_per_year |> mutate(selected = rate)
)

title: 3  Selection scenarios
section: 3.2 Which rate moves the trait fastest?
text:
3.2 Which rate moves the trait fastest?






ImportantYour turn — predict first



Same species, same heritability, same selection strength — only the target vital rate differs. Which of fertility, juvenile survival, adult survival or maturation do you think will drive the fastest genetic change per year? Commit to a ranking before you look.



ggplot(prop_all, aes(year, M_EBVS, colour = selected)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = vital_pal, labels = vital_lab, name = "Selection on") +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Mean breeding value",
       title = "Same population, four places for selection to act")







Figure 3.1: Mean breeding value through time for species 3, under selection on each of the four vital rates. The steeper the climb, the faster the adaptation.





The slopes differ markedly. To compare them as numbers, each run already reports the realised adaptation rate per year in out$V:



Table 3.1

  selected     = rates,
  rate_label   = vital_lab[rates],
  per_year     = map_dbl(runs, "V"),
  gen_time     = map_dbl(runs, "T_GEN")
) |>
  mutate(per_generation = per_year * gen_time) |>
  arrange(desc(per_year))

  selected rate_label              per_year gen_time per_generation
  <chr>    <chr>                      <dbl>    <dbl>          <dbl>
1 SJ       Juvenile survival (S_J)  0.00688     6.30         0.0433
2 Fe       Fertility (F)            0.00497     6.30         0.0313
3 SA       Adult survival (S_A)     0.00365     6.30         0.0230
4 Y        Maturation (γ)           0.00224     6.30         0.0141





adapt_rate |>
  ggplot(aes(reorder(rate_label, per_year), per_year, fill = selected)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = vital_pal, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Adaptation rate per year (\u0394 breeding value)",
       title = "Selection on juvenile survival adapts fastest here")







Figure 3.2: Realised adaptation rate per year by selected vital rate (species 3).











TipKey idea



For most life histories, a trait acting on juvenile survival drives the fastest per-year adaptation, with fertility close behind — because both feed directly into recruitment, the part of the life cycle selection can turn over quickly. Selection on adult survival is the slowest to register, especially in short-lived species. Hold this thought: in Chapter 4 it gets overturned.








WarningHeads-up — Beta is on the link scale



The selection strength Beta lives on the logit/log scale of each vital rate, so a fixed Beta = 0.15 is not the same biological pressure across rates or species. That is deliberate — it is why the original study reports several definitions of adaptation rate (Chapter 5) — but it means you should compare scenarios qualitatively here, not read the bar heights as absolute selection.

text:
3.3 Your turn — change the species






ImportantExercise



Re-run the four scenarios for the albatross (species 5) by calling run_scenario(rate, sp = 5) across rates. Does the ranking of vital rates change? Which rate now adapts fastest per year?

tibble(
  rate_label = vital_lab[rates],
  per_year   = map_dbl(runs5, "V")

For the long-lived albatross, selection on adult survival is no longer last — in long-lived species, adult survival carries much of the reproductive value, so a trait there matters more. The “best” vital rate to target is not universal; it depends on where the species sits on the slow–fast continuum, which is exactly the next chapter.

section: 4.2 Project every species under every selection scenario

title: 4  The slow–fast continuum
text:
4.3 The same result, two definitions
Now the heart of the matter. We plot the realised adaptation rate two ways — per year and per generation — and the story changes completely.

res |>
  select(sp, rate, `per year` = per_year, `per generation` = per_gen) |>
  pivot_longer(c(`per year`, `per generation`),
               names_to = "unit", values_to = "rate_value") |>
  mutate(unit = factor(unit, levels = c("per year", "per generation"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(sp, rate_value, fill = rate)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge2(), width = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~unit, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = vital_pal, labels = vital_lab, name = "Selection on") +
  labs(x = "Species (fast → slow)", y = "Adaptation rate",
       title = "Who adapts fastest? It depends how you ask")







Figure 4.1: Adaptation rate across the slow–fast continuum (species 1 = fastest, 5 = slowest), under selection on each vital rate. Left: per year. Right: per generation. The same 20 runs tell two different stories.





Read the two panels against each other:

Per year (left): adaptation generally slows down as you move from fast to slow species — an albatross changes less per calendar year than a grass. But note the exception for adult survival, where intermediate species can peak.
Per generation (right): the picture rearranges. For some vital rates the slow species now look as adaptable or more so, because each of their generations is worth many years.

title: 4  The slow–fast continuum
text:
4.4 The cleanest demonstration: fertility
Zoom in on selection acting on fertility alone:

res |>
  filter(rate == "Fe") |>
  select(sp, `per year` = per_year, `per generation` = per_gen) |>
  pivot_longer(-sp, names_to = "unit", values_to = "rate_value") |>
  ggplot(aes(sp, rate_value, group = unit, colour = unit)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("per year" = "#B5651D", "per generation" = "#3E6E83"),
                      name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Species (fast → slow)", y = "Adaptation rate",
       title = "Fertility selection: a textbook result")







Figure 4.2: Selection on fertility only. Per year, adaptation falls steeply with generation time. Per generation, it is essentially flat — every species adapts the same amount per generation.





This is not a quirk of the simulation — it falls straight out of the theory. When selection acts on fertility, the per-generation rate reduces to \(h^2 V_P\,\beta\), which contains no species-specific term at all. Per year you then divide by generation time, so the slow species lag. (We derive and check this in Chapter 5.)






TipKey idea — the punchline



There is no universal answer to “which species adapts fastest.” It depends on (1) the species’ life cycle, (2) which vital rate selection targets, and (3) how you define adaptation — per year or per generation, and in what units of selection. The original study makes exactly this point: don’t assume an answer from intuition; model the rate with the definition that matters to your question, and read off the number (Van de Walle et al. 2025).








ImportantYour turn



Your prediction from Chapter 1 — grass versus albatross — was about adaptation per year. Look at the left panel: were you right? Now look at the right panel. Did the albatross “lose” on both definitions, or only one? Which definition would a conservation manager planning over calendar years care about, and which would a quantitative geneticist reach for?








CautionDiscussion — there isn’t one right answer





A manager allocating effort over the next few decades thinks in years, so the per-year panel is their world: fast species adapt more in the time available. A quantitative geneticist studying the genetic response thinks in generations, where the breeder’s equation lives — and there the slow albatross is far from hopeless. Both are correct; they are answering different questions. Recognising which definition a claim rests on is half the battle in cross-disciplinary work on adaptation.



You have now done the core of the workshop: you can run the model, read it, and reason about its central result. The next part opens the engine for those who want it.

title: 5  Under the hood
text:
5.1 Three dimensions instead of one
This part is for the curious. None of it is needed to use MPM() — but understanding the machine makes you trust its outputs and bend it to new questions.
A classic MPM tracks individuals by stage only — a vector of (juveniles, adults). The EvoDemo-Hyper MPM tracks them by stage × breeding value × phenotype: a three-dimensional hyperstate (Roth and Caswell 2016). Each cell counts the individuals that are, say, “adult, with breeding value class 12, expressing phenotype class 15”.
The full projection matrix factorises into a survival part \(\tilde{\mathbf{U}}\) and a reproduction part \(\tilde{\mathbf{F}}\),
\[
\mathbf{n}_{t+1} = \tilde{\mathbf{A}}[\mathbf{n}_t]\,\mathbf{n}_t,
\qquad
\tilde{\mathbf{A}} = \tilde{\mathbf{U}} + \tilde{\mathbf{F}},
\]
and each of those is built by applying one process per dimension, shuffling the population vector between steps with vec-permutation matrices so that each block acts on the right axis (Hunter and Caswell 2005). The package handles all of this; the result is just sparse-matrix multiplication.

title: 5  Under the hood
text:
5.2 The building blocks
The hyperstate matrix is assembled from a few tiny operations. Here they are — the same definitions the model uses internally — so you can see exactly how the machine is put together. We define them here so this chapter is self-contained:

Emat <- function(i, j, u) {                 # a matrix of zeros with a single 1 at (i, j)
  E <- matrix(0, nrow = u, ncol = u)
  E[i, j] <- 1
  E
}

speye <- function(N) {                      # a sparse identity matrix
  Matrix::sparseMatrix(i = 1:N, j = 1:N, x = rep(1, N))
}

GVLE <- function(zz, Va) {                  # the Mendelian segregation kernel
  exp(-(zz^2) / Va) / sqrt(pi * Va)
}

BD_proj_mat <- function(B) {                # assemble a block-diagonal matrix from an array of blocks
  siz <- dim(B)[-1]
  s   <- prod(siz)
  sk  <- s / siz[1]
  siz <- siz[2:3]
  A   <- matrix(0, nrow = s, ncol = s)
  for (i in 1:sk) {
    r <- ((i - 1) %% siz[1]) + 1
    c <- floor((i - 1) / siz[1]) + 1
    A <- A + kronecker(Emat(i, i, sk), B[, , r, c])
  }
  A
}

Emat() places a single 1 in an otherwise empty matrix — the atom of the block-diagonal construction:

Emat(2, 3, 4)

     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,]    0    0    0    0
[2,]    0    0    1    0
[3,]    0    0    0    0
[4,]    0    0    0    0


speye() makes a sparse identity (breeding value and phenotype are assumed fixed within a lifetime, so their within-life transition matrices are identities):

as.matrix(speye(3))

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    0    0
[2,]    0    1    0
[3,]    0    0    1


And BD_proj_mat() assembles a block-diagonal matrix from an array of blocks — the operation behind \(\mathbb{U}, \mathbb{B}, \mathbb{P}\) and friends:

toy <- array(runif(2 * 2 * 3 * 3, 1, 8), dim = c(2, 2, 3, 3))
image(BD_proj_mat(toy), main = "Block-diagonal structure")







Figure 5.1: A block-diagonal matrix built by BD_proj_mat() from a 2×2×3×3 array of blocks. This sparse structure is what makes the model fast.

title: 5  Under the hood
text:
5.3 Where inheritance enters
Offspring do not copy a parent’s breeding value — they sample one. Under the Fisher infinitesimal model, an offspring’s breeding value is drawn from a normal distribution centred on the mid-parent value, with variance equal to half the additive genetic variance. The function GVLE() defined above is exactly this segregation kernel:

zz <- seq(-2, 2, by = 0.05)
tibble(z = zz, density = GVLE(zz, Va = 0.2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(z, density)) +
  geom_area(fill = species_pal["3"], alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, colour = species_pal["4"]) +
  labs(x = "Offspring breeding value (relative to mid-parent)", y = "Density",
       title = "Inheritance as a convolution")







Figure 5.2: The Mendelian segregation kernel GVLE(): the spread of offspring breeding values around the mid-parent value, for Va = 0.2.





Each year the model convolves the parental breeding-value distribution with this kernel — that single step is the entire evolutionary engine.

title: 5  Under the hood
text:
5.4 Six ways to define “adaptation rate”
A recurring theme of the workshop is that adaptation rate is not one number. The paper lays out six definitions built from two choices:

Time unit — per year (RAT) or per generation (RAG).
Selection unit — on the linear/link scale (\(\beta\)), per unit of the vital rate (\(\theta\)), or per unit of individual fitness (\(R_0\)): giving \(RA_{S\theta}\) and \(RA_{SR_0}\) variants.

Their punchline: under the most standardised definition (per generation, per unit of fitness), the rate collapses to \(h^2 V_P\) — identical for every species and every vital rate. Strip away the standardisation and the differences between species reappear. The “disagreement” between fields was largely a disagreement about units (Van de Walle et al. 2025).

title: 5  Under the hood
section: 5.5 Does the matrix model match the theory?
text:
5.5 Does the matrix model match the theory?
This is the validation that earns trust. We compute the analytic per-year rate (RAT) for all five species under each vital rate, then overlay the realised rate from running MPM().

theory <- species |>
  mutate(th = pmap(list(F, SA, SJ, Y = gamma),
                   \(F, SA, SJ, Y) theoretical_rates(F, SA, SJ, Y, Va = 0.2, beta = 0.15))) |>
  select(species, th) |>
  unnest(th) |>
  select(species, rate, theory_year = per_year)


project_one <- function(sp, rate) {
  MPM(h2 = 0.2, Vp = 1, Beta = 0.15,
      Fe = species$F[sp], SA = species$SA[sp], SJ = species$SJ[sp],
      S0 = species$SJ[sp], Y = species$gamma[sp], selectedrate = rate)
}

mpm <- expand_grid(species = factor(1:5), rate = c("Fe", "SJ", "SA", "Y")) |>
  mutate(mpm_year = map2_dbl(as.integer(species), rate, \(s, r) project_one(s, r)$V))

compare <- left_join(mpm, theory, by = c("species", "rate"))


ggplot(compare, aes(species)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = mpm_year, fill = rate), alpha = 0.55, width = 0.7) +
  geom_point(aes(y = theory_year), size = 2, colour = "grey15") +
  facet_wrap(~rate, scales = "free_y", labeller = as_labeller(vital_lab)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = vital_pal, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Species (fast → slow)", y = "Adaptation rate per year",
       title = "Simulation (bars) vs analytic theory (points)")







Figure 5.3: Per-year adaptation rate: bars are the realised values from MPM(), points are the analytic theory. They line up across species and vital rates — the matrix model is doing what the maths says it should.











TipKey idea



The matrix model is not a black box that replaces theory — it agrees with it, and then keeps working in the many cases where closed-form formulas run out (non-Gaussian trait distributions, evolving variances, plasticity). That is the whole argument for the approach.

title: 5  Under the hood
section: 5.6 Tuning and the artefacts to watch
text:
5.6 Tuning and the artefacts to watch
A few arguments control the numerical grid. Used carelessly they produce believable-looking nonsense, so it pays to know them.

g — number of breeding-value/phenotype classes (default 20). More classes = finer resolution but slower (≈ 1 s at g = 10, ≈ 8 s at g = 40). The paper used 40.
xp — the half-range of trait values, i.e. the grid spans \([-x_p, x_p]\) (default 4).
timeA — number of years projected (default 100).







WarningHeads-up — the boundary artefact



If the trait adapts far enough to reach the edge of the grid, the distribution piles up against the boundary and the adaptation rate becomes unreliable. The fix is to give it more room (xp) or fewer years (timeA). The model warns you when the genetic distribution is too narrow or too wide for the chosen grid — read those warnings.



# A deliberately under-resolved setup: very low heritability on a coarse grid.
risky <- MPM(g = 20, xp = 2, h2 = 0.01, Beta = 0.15,
             Fe = species$F[4], SA = species$SA[4], SJ = species$SJ[4],
             S0 = species$SJ[4], Y = species$gamma[4],
             enforce_initial_lambda1 = TRUE)

Warning in MPM(g = 20, xp = 2, h2 = 0.01, Beta = 0.15, Fe = species$F[4], : g
is probably too low given h2 and xp. There are not enough breeding value
classes to house Va below (xp/g)^2. Check estimates of Va and Vp in the output
to see the realised h2. You may increase xp or decrease g.


I have adjusted Fe to 0.298712871287129 because the enforce_initial_lambda1 is set to TRUE.

The realised additive variance drifts away from the requested value: some of this is genuine erosion of variance under selection, but some is the grid being too coarse to represent a narrow distribution. Always check Va and Vp in properties_per_year against what you asked for.
Two more useful switches:

enforce_initial_lambda1 = TRUE adjusts fertility so the population starts at \(\lambda = 1\) (a stationary baseline) — handy when you want to isolate evolution from raw growth.
stabilise_population_structure = FALSE starts away from the stable stage distribution, letting you observe transient demographic oscillations before equilibrium.

title: 6  Export & extend
text:
6.1 Getting things out as PDF
There are two senses of “PDF output”, and the workshop gives you both.
The whole workshop as a PDF. Use the Download PDF link in the sidebar — Quarto renders this entire site to a single document from the same source you have been reading.
A figure as a vector PDF. For your own results, ggsave() writes a clean, scalable PDF you can drop straight into a manuscript. Build the figure once, then save it:
out <- MPM(h2 = 0.2, Vp = 1, Beta = 0.15,
           Fe = species$F[3], SA = species$SA[3], SJ = species$SJ[3],
           S0 = species$SJ[3], Y = species$gamma[3], selectedrate = "SJ")

p <- out$pheno_distribution |>
  filter(year %in% seq(1, 101, by = 25)) |>
  ggplot(aes(phenotypic_midvalue, density, colour = factor(year))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "mako", direction = -1, name = "Year") +
  labs(x = "Phenotype value", y = "Density",
       title = "Passerine under juvenile-survival selection")
p
ggsave("my_figure.pdf", p, width = 7, height = 4.2, device = cairo_pdf)
A full parameterised report. The repository ships a template at templates/report.qmd. Render it to PDF for any species and selection scenario without editing the file — just pass parameters:
quarto::quarto_render(
  "templates/report.qmd",
  execute_params = list(species_id = 5, rate = "SA", beta = 0.3, h2 = 0.2)
)
This is the reproducible way to hand a collaborator a tidy PDF for a specific run: the parameters are recorded in the document itself.

title: 6  Export & extend
text:
6.2 Extending the model
The two-stage life cycle with one trait is a teaching scaffold. The same framework reaches further — here is where to look next, all grounded in the original paper (Van de Walle et al. 2025).
Phenotypic plasticity. In the base model an individual keeps its phenotype for life (the within-life phenotype-transition matrices \(\mathbf{P}_{ij}\) are identities). Make them non-identity and a trait can change with age or with the environment — that is plasticity, expressed in exactly the same matrix language as evolution.
Two-sex inheritance. The model already tracks male and female breeding values, so paternal contributions are not ignored — a known shortcoming of several earlier evolutionary IPMs. Keep this in mind when comparing results to single-sex frameworks.
Evolving genetic variance. The base model holds \(V_A\), \(V_P\) and \(h^2\) at birth constant. The authors note that letting \(V_A\) vary is computationally cheap to add, though it requires committing to assumptions about genetic architecture.
Richer life cycles. Nothing restricts the demography to two stages. The vec-permutation construction scales to any stage-structured life cycle — including the kinds of long-lived marine and terrestrial vertebrates these methods were built for.

title: 6  Export & extend
text:
6.3 Capstone — your turn






ImportantA question to take home



Pick a species you actually study (or the closest of our five). Decide which vital rate selection most plausibly acts on, and which definition of adaptation rate answers your real question — per year for a management horizon, per generation for a genetic one. Run it, plot the trait distribution through time, and export a one-figure PDF. You now have a reproducible eco-evolutionary projection for your system — and a clear-eyed sense of what its adaptation rate does and does not mean.
